passages.title: A Failed Talk
passages.text: A talk is a good way to explain some concept. When doing a talk you need to know your audience, you can't target beginners and advanced users at once A failed talk can happen for many reason wrong subject bad slides/content wrong audience targeting Substack There are no hard subjects to be cover in a presentation, there are only different ways of presenting them. I did a “bad” talk at Rancho Dev when I’ve talked about Forms and Formik (slides and code here). The problem of this talk was about my assumptions of the audience. I’m used to talking in places that most people know basic React concepts, but Rancho Dev conf was a more broad conferences with many different topics. As I did not provide more context (a basic intro of React, react hooks and so on), it was hard to explain to them how to apply this concepts to solve the forms in React land. I always ask for feedback give me here) after my talk, and this one I received a really bad one saying that I thought the audience won’t grasp the concepts. The truth was that I didn’t understand really well these concepts to explain like I’m 5. How would be a better talk for that audience? More about the problem and motivation (how hard complex forms can be to get right) basic React intro concepts more concepts less code

passages.title: Build Less
passages.text: monorepo testing and build playground Tooling around Git and compare url to decide what to build It does not matter if you have the fastest algorithm if your N is too big. Sometimes you need to reduce N to make sure you sure things does not grow with N. As your project grows, your "N" will grow together. Your dependencies sizes will grow Your codebase will grow Your tests will grow (if you care about long term) Your build process will slow down as you are building more code. Your type checking will get slower. One way to solve this is to use a directly acyclic graph (DAG) to avoid testing, type checking, rebuilding what has not changed since last time. In this article we won't use a DAG, we are going to use a much simpler strategy that can be modify to add a DAG to make it more robust. The first thing that we want to do is to only run tests that are affected by the current files. How do we know which files were changed? We are going to use some git commands to make this possible. CircleCI concepts CircleCI is a continuous integration system that let you automate common software tasks, for instance: linting, tests, type checking, build, deploy. A new pipeline is trigged when you do some work (push a new commit, for instance). A pipeline can contains many workflows. Each workflow have jobs that represents the cycle of your software process (for instance, install test deploy). A

passages.title: Build Less
passages.text: job contains N steps of commands to perform something, like run lint, run tests. Compare URL CircleCI had a concept of CIRCLECI COMPARE URL before v2.1, that you can recreate in v2.1 using pipeline variables, like this: environment: CIRCLE COMPARE URL: << pipeline.project.git url /compare/<< pipeline.git.base revision ...<<pipeline.git.revision Here is a few examples of COMPARE URL: The url above says that this pipeline contains code from the base branch (master or main) to the a2e2709c4 commit. The above contains code from commit 37ac69404a5b to 69bc6e3fe337 Test by yourself here Problems with CIRLCLE COMPARE URL using pipeline variables The first problem we hit when using CIRCLE COMPARE URL using pipeline variables was that they are only bringing the range from the current commit to the last commit. We would like to always test files related to the whole changes in the pull requests. To fix this, we discard the "base revision" (the first commit in the compare url), and use the base branch instead. this turns into Before getting the files using git diff (spoiler), we need to checkout the latest master. This is needed because CircleCI only do a shallow checkout to make it faster, you don't need all git history or branches in every pipeline.
